entries.title: Building
entries.summary: Open the build menu with B, set a frame down where you want it, then bring the materials and install them by hand, one part at a time.

sections.text: Nothing is built by magic. A blueprint gives you a frame - a pale outline of the finished piece - and the frame becomes real only as you fit the actual poles, sticks, boards, cord, earth and straw into it. Every part you install is the very item you carried, and every part comes back if you take the piece apart.

steps: Press [key]B[/key] and choose a blueprint. The panel shows what it needs, and how much of each you are carrying.
Press [b]Place this frame[/b]. A ghost of the piece follows your view: pale blue where it can go, red where it can't, with the reason shown below.
[key]R[/key] turns it a quarter turn when it has snapped to something, 15° otherwise; the [key]Wheel[/key] turns it 15° either way.
[key]LMB[/key] sets the frame down. Placing a frame costs nothing. You stay in build mode to place another; [key]RMB[/key], [key]Esc[/key] or [key]B[/key] leaves.

sections.text: Look at a frame: it tells you how many of its parts are in and what it still needs, and the next part glows faintly. Hold that item and hold [key]LMB[/key] on the frame. Depending on the part you hammer in poles, lash on cordage, weave in sticks or straw, daub on earth or clay, or thatch with straw. Parts go in a fixed order. Anyone can help, and a frame doesn't have to be finished in one go.

list: [b]Wooden platform[/b] (a 2 × 2 m deck): 2 poles, 6 boards, 2 cordage.
[b]Support post[/b]: 1 pole, 1 cordage.
[b]Railing[/b]: 2 sticks, 1 pole, 1 cordage.
[b]Ladder[/b]: 2 poles, 5 sticks, 2 cordage.
[b]Wattle wall[/b]: 3 poles, 6 sticks, 6 loads of earth or lumps of raw clay.
[b]Doorway wall[/b]: 3 poles, 4 sticks, 4 loads of earth or lumps of raw clay.
[b]Thatch roof[/b]: 2 poles, 3 sticks, 8 straw, 1 cordage.
[b]Storage shelf[/b] (a raised surface to set things on): 4 sticks, 2 boards, 1 cordage.
[b]Sleeping mat[/b]: 6 straw, 1 cordage.
Platforms snap to the edges of other platforms; otherwise they sit on the ground.
Walls, doorway walls and railings snap along platform edges, or stand on the ground.
Posts go under the corners and edges of platforms. Where a corner hangs over the abyss, the post slants back to the cliff as a brace.
A roof sits on top of the walls around a platform.

Aim a ladder at a wall or a platform edge to lean it there. Press [key]E[/key] to climb, [key]W[/key] and [key]S[/key] to go up and down, and keep pushing forward at the top to step off. [key]Space[/key] or [key]E[/key] lets go.
Nothing can be built hard up against the tree, the outcrop, a boulder or the flat stone, inside another piece, or buried in the ground.

sections.text: A piece only becomes solid - something to stand on, lean on, shelter under or hold weight - once its last part is in. Until then it is just a frame.

sections.warn: Anything that has been in a fire is no good for building. And nothing can be built where nothing would hold it up - see [b]What holds it up[/b].

entries.title: Platforms and the edge
entries.summary: Wooden platforms extend the island out over the abyss, one two-meter step at a time and only as far as something holds them up. Railings keep you on them.

sections.text: A platform is a 2 × 2 meter deck of six rough boards on two pole beams, lashed with cordage. On solid ground it's a floor. Built out from the island's rim, it gives you room the island never had - with a long drop beneath your feet.

steps: Start with a platform resting on the island near the rim: the ground carries it.
Place the next one snapped to its outer edge. Hanging over the abyss, it is one step out - and that holds.
A platform two steps out creaks and sags. Put a post or a brace under it.
Three steps out isn't allowed at all - unless a post or brace somewhere underneath has reset the count.

sections.text: A platform resting on a finished post or wall that stands on solid ground counts as carried by the ground. Over the abyss, a post placed under a corner close to the cliff slants back to it as a brace. Brace the first platform out, and you can go two more steps beyond it. See [b]What holds it up[/b].
A railing is a waist-high rail along a platform edge: two sticks, a pole and a cordage. Once it is finished it is solid, and it stops you walking off. A sensible thing to have above an abyss.

sections.warn: When a platform collapses, its boards, poles and cord fall - along with whatever was on it. Over the abyss, all of it is gone forever, and so are you if you were standing on it.

sections.tip: Crouch with [key]Ctrl[/key] while you work on an open edge, and put the railing up before anything else.

entries.title: What holds it up
entries.summary: Every finished piece must be held up by the ground, by something the ground holds, or by a post. One platform step out over nothing holds, two creaks, three is refused - and a piece that loses its support groans for about ten seconds, then falls.

sections.text: The rule is simple: how far is this deck from something solid? A finished piece is supported if it rests on the island, or touches another piece that is supported. Weight travels through platforms, posts and walls; railings and roofs simply rest on what is beneath them.

list: [b]Carried by the ground[/b]: anything resting on the island, any post or wall standing on it, and any platform resting on such a post or wall.
[b]One step out[/b]: a platform joined to a carried one but hanging over nothing - a two-meter cantilever. Fine.
[b]Two steps out[/b]: it creaks under its own weight and sags. It holds, but you'll be told that a post or brace beneath would steady it.
[b]Three steps out[/b]: it can't hold, and you won't be allowed to place it.

sections.text: A support post - a pole and a cordage - under a platform corner carries it if the post's foot stands on solid ground. Where the corner hangs over the abyss, the post slants back to the top of the cliff as a brace, its foot planted at the rim. Either way the platform above counts as carried by the ground again, and you can build further out from there. A brace only reaches back so far, though: the corner must be within about 1.7 meters of the cliff top, so it's the platforms nearest the island that can be braced.

Support is worked out again whenever a piece is finished or changed. If something no longer has a way down to the ground - its post was taken apart, or the platform it hung from - it starts groaning and shifting, and everyone nearby is warned. About ten seconds later it collapses, and every part it was made of falls where it is.

list: Only finished pieces carry anything. A frame, even one part short, holds nothing up.
Taking even one part off a finished piece turns it back into a frame: whatever relied on it loses that support at once.
Pieces have to touch to share the load.

sections.warn: When you hear groaning, get off. If you can finish a post underneath in time it will hold; if not, it falls - and over the abyss, its parts are gone for good.

entries.title: Shelter
entries.summary: Walls keep the wind off and a roof keeps the rain off. Together they keep you warmer and drier, and keep drying pottery and compost out of the rain.

sections.text: Shelter here is physical: what matters is whether there is something solid over your head, and how many directions around you are blocked. It doesn't have to look like a house - but a house does it best.

A wattle wall is three poles hammered upright, six sticks woven between them, and six loads of earth or lumps of raw clay daubed on. Anything solid within three meters of you - a wall, rock, the trunk of the great tree, a high bank of earth - blocks the wind from that side. Fully surrounded, you feel only a fifth of the wind's chill.
A doorway wall has an opening ninety centimeters wide and 1.9 meters tall to walk through, and needs two fewer sticks and two fewer loads of daub than a full wall. Leave yourself a way in.

A thatch roof - two pole rafters, three sticks, eight bundles of straw and a cordage - sits on top of the walls around a platform. Under any finished piece overhead you are sheltered: you stay dry in the rain, and you are 2.5 °C warmer, or up to 5 °C with walls all around.

list: [b]You[/b]: warmer, out of the wind, and dry.
[b]Drying pottery[/b]: under a roof, rain can't reach it.
[b]Fires[/b]: a roof keeps the rain from chilling them.
[b]Compost[/b]: a covered heap doesn't get rained on - so water it yourself.
[b]Wood and grass[/b] laid out to dry stay out of the rain too.

steps: Choose a spot, on the ground or on a platform.
Put walls up on three or four sides, with a doorway wall in one of them.
Lay a sleeping mat inside, and keep a fire burning close by.

sections.warn: A roof needs something to rest on, and walls need the ground or a deck beneath them - see [b]What holds it up[/b].

entries.title: Taking things apart
entries.summary: Nothing you build is permanent. Take any piece apart from the build menu and every part comes back to you as the item it was made from.

steps: Press [key]B[/key] and choose [b]Take apart...[/b] at the top of the build menu.
Look at a piece and hold [key]LMB[/key]. Parts come off one at a time, last in first, about two a second, each straight into your pack.
When the last part is off, the empty frame disappears.

sections.text: Every part comes back just as it went in: the same poles and boards, the very earth or clay you daubed on. Nothing is lost.

list: Taking even one part off a finished piece makes it a frame again: it stops carrying anything, and whatever rested on it may start to groan.
Taking apart a sleeping mat clears it as anyone's waking place.
Make room in your pack first. A part that doesn't fit drops where the piece stands - and over the abyss, that means gone.
Taking apart only works from the build menu, so nobody pulls up a floor by accident.

sections.tip: Moving house? Take it apart, carry the parts, and build it again. Frames are free; only the parts cost anything.
